plan.contextChunk: This figure shows two fragments of a recursion tree side by side, labeled (a) and (b), with nodes carrying subproblem sizes. In (a) a top node labeled n has two branches: the left ends at a bare 0 with no box drawn around it, the right at a node labeled n-1. A large pale gray ellipse encloses the top node and the n-1 node together, and a heavy dotted arrow runs from that ellipse rightward to the expression Theta(n). The n-1 node branches in turn to two gray rectangles reading (n-1)/2 - 1 and (n-1)/2. In (b) a single node labeled n is ringed by a small pale gray ellipse, again with a dotted arrow pointing right to Theta(n), and it branches to two gray rectangles that both read (n-1)/2. The shared Theta(n) tag is the point of the comparison: the shaded groupings cost the same in each panel, while the boxed subproblems still waiting differ. Putting a lopsided split followed by an even one beside a single even split motivates the argument that alternating bad and good partitions costs about what uninterrupted good partitioning would.

interactionPlan.concept: Alternating bad and good partitions in quicksort produces recursion-tree levels whose total cost is Θ(n) per grouping — the same as an uninterrupted balanced split — so the overall running time stays Θ(n log n).

demo_steps.title: The bad-good fragment
demo_steps.narration: In panel (a), a worst-case split n → 0 and n-1 is immediately followed by an even split of n-1. The gray ellipse groups both levels of partitioning work and costs Θ(n) total.

demo_steps.title: What one grouping costs
demo_steps.narration: Click the shaded ellipse: the n and n-1 nodes brighten together — this pair of levels is being charged as a single Θ(n) of work, with two boxed subproblems still waiting below.

demo_steps.title: The balanced fragment
demo_steps.narration: Switch to panel (b): one balanced split n → (n-1)/2 twice, also costing Θ(n) for its level. Both panels spend the same Θ(n) but end with subproblems of size at most (n-1)/2.

demo_steps.title: Expand and compare
demo_steps.narration: Press expand to push the recursion deeper: bad splits make the tree taller but never more than double the balanced depth, because every bad level is absorbed into a Θ(n) grouping with the good level that follows it.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: A bad split followed by a good split costs Θ(n) for both levels combined and leaves subproblems no larger than a single good split would — so alternating luck changes only the constant factor, never the Θ(n log n) total.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Two tree fragments side by side on white background, panel labels (a) and (b) centered beneath. Nodes are small ovals with italic serif labels (n, n-1, 0); waiting subproblems are light gray rectangles with italic serif labels ((n-1)/2 - 1, (n-1)/2). Edges are plain thin black lines angled down-left and down-right. The cost grouping is a large pale gray translucent ellipse tilted to enclose the n and n-1 ovals in panel (a), and a small horizontal ellipse around just n in panel (b). A heavy dotted black arrow runs horizontally rightward from each ellipse to a large Θ(n) label aligned at the same height in both panels — this shared Θ(n) tag is the visual anchor of the comparison. On click, ellipse contents brighten (increase node label weight / saturation); on expand, new child boxes fade in below with the accumulated cost label updating beside the Θ(n) tag.

authoredContext:
In the average case, PARTITION produces a mix of “good” and “bad” splits. In a recursion tree for an average-case execution of PARTITION, the good and bad splits are distributed randomly throughout the tree. Suppose, for the sake of intuition, that the good and bad splits alternate levels in the tree, and that the good splits are best-case splits and the bad splits are worst-case splits. Figure 7.5(a) shows the splits at two consecutive levels in the recursion tree. At the root of the tree, the cost is n for partitioning, and the subarrays produced have sizes n 1 and 0: the worst case. At the next level, the subarray of size n 1 undergoes best-case partitioning into subarrays of size .n 1/=2 1 and .n 1/=2. Let’s assume that the boundary-condition cost is 1 for the subarray of size 0. The combination of the bad split followed by the good split produces three subarrays of sizes 0, .n  1/=2  1, and .n  1/=2 at a combined partitioning cost
of ‚.n/ C ‚.n  1/ D ‚.n/. Certainly, this situation is no worse than that in
Figure 7.5(b), namely a single level of partitioning that produces two subarrays of
size .n  1/=2, at a cost of ‚.n/. Yet this latter situation is balanced! Intuitively,
the ‚.n  1/ cost of the bad split can be absorbed into the ‚.n/ cost of the good
split, and the resulting split is good. Thus, the running time of quicksort, when levels alternate between good and bad splits, is like the running time for good splits
alone: still O.n lg n/, but with a slightly larger constant hidden by the O-notation.
We shall give a rigorous analysis of the expected running time of a randomized
version of quicksort in Section 7.4.2.

evaluation.notes: Both panels are present with correct topology, node labels, boxes, ellipses, and dotted Θ(n) arrows, and the step player, expand-levels button, and ellipse highlight interaction are all functional and pedagogically on-point; main issues are the clipped/extraneous 'Σ so far' caption and a slightly undersized grouping ellipse in panel (a).
